book: Loading, Running SQL and Checking a Reproduction

1.q: Look at the code on the screen. What does the chunksize argument change about what read csv returns?
opts: One data frame, but the file is read five thousand bytes at a time
An iterator of data frames, five thousand rows each, instead of one data frame
Only the first five thousand rows, as a quick preview of the file
The whole file split into five thousand equal parts, after it is read into memory
1.why: With a chunk size, read csv returns an iterator. Each step of the loop gives the next block of rows, so memory holds one block at a time.
1.code:
for chunk in pd.read_csv(path, dtype=str,
                         keep_default_na=False,
                         chunksize=5000):
    rows = convert(chunk)
    con.executemany(insert, rows)

2.q: Why does the real loader send rows to SQLite in batches of a hundred thousand, rather than all at once?
opts: SQLite rejects any single insert call with more than a hundred thousand rows
Batches let SQLite build its indexes in parallel while the rows keep arriving
Smaller batches make it easier for SQLite to guess each column's type correctly
Memory then holds one batch at a time, whatever the size of the file
2.why: The Forbes file has about six million rows. Batching keeps memory flat, and each batch still goes in with one call.

3.q: Look at the code on the screen. What would go wrong if you deleted the last two lines?
opts: The leftover rows after the last full batch would never be inserted
Nothing, because the loop already inserts every batch, including the last one
The count would be right, but the last batch would be inserted twice
The table would be empty, because execute many only commits on the final call
3.why: Inside the loop a batch is sent only when it is full. The leftover rows after the loop need one more call. The loader's final count check would catch the gap.
3.code:
batch = []
for row in reader:
    batch.append([cast(v) for cast, v
                  in zip(casts, row)])
    if len(batch) >= BATCH:
        con.executemany(insert, batch)
        n += len(batch)
        batch = []
con.executemany(insert, batch)
n += len(batch)

1.q: The raw file writes a missing worth as an empty field. Which Python value makes SQLite store a real null?
opts: An empty string
The string NULL
None
Zero
1.why: The SQLite driver turns None into null. An empty string is stored as a value, and the string NULL is just text.

2.q: Look at the code on the screen. Why strip the spaces before testing for an empty field?
opts: A field of only spaces is missing too, and readr trims spaces the same way
Strip turns an empty string into None, so the test after it is only a safety net
Float refuses any string with spaces around it, so strip is needed for the conversion
SQLite stores trailing spaces as a separate type, which would break the sums
2.why: R's read csv trims spaces by default, and Python's readers do not. Stripping first makes a blank field null and keeps text equal to R's. Float itself accepts surrounding spaces.
2.code:
v = v.strip(" \t")
row.append(float(v) if v != "" else None)

3.q: A loader reads with pandas' defaults. Someone's name in the file is the word null. What happens to it?
opts: It is kept as the text null, because only empty fields become missing values
Pandas raises an error, because a text column cannot hold a missing value
It becomes None in pandas, and then the string None in SQLite
Pandas turns it into N a N, so the name arrives in SQLite as a null
3.why: By default pandas treats several strings as missing, null among them. Reading with d type string and keep default n a false keeps them as text.

1.q: Look at the code on the screen. The file holds eight statements. What happens?
opts: Python raises an error, because execute runs exactly one statement
Only the first statement runs, and the other seven are silently ignored
All eight run, because execute splits the text at each semicolon
All eight run, but none of them is saved until you call commit
1.why: Execute refuses more than one statement with an error. A file of statements needs execute script.

2.q: Execute script hits an error in the fifth statement. What state is the database in?
opts: Nothing has changed, because execute script rolls back the whole script
Every statement except the fifth has run, since it skips the one that failed
The first four statements have run, and their changes stay
The database is locked until you call rollback on the connection
2.why: Execute script runs statements in order and stops at the first error. What ran before it stays. That is why each block starts with drop table if exists.

3.q: Look at the code on the screen. Why is this a bad use of execute script?
opts: Execute script cannot run a delete statement, only create table and drop table statements
No placeholders, so typed input lands inside the SQL and can add statements
The semicolon at the end makes execute script run the delete twice
Input returns bytes, and execute script cannot read bytes as SQL text
3.why: Execute script has no placeholders, so it is for trusted files only. For values, use execute with a question mark.
3.code:
fid = input("id to delete: ")
sql = ("DELETE FROM rtb_ca_cik "
       f"WHERE forbes_id = '{fid}';")
con.executescript(sql)

1.q: In the loader's insert statement, what do the question marks stand for?
opts: Columns whose type SQLite should guess from the first row it receives
Optional values that a row is allowed to leave out
Wildcards that match any column name in the table
Placeholders that SQLite fills from each row given to execute many
1.why: Each question mark is a parameter. The values travel separately, and SQLite handles quoting, types and None.

2.q: Look at the code on the screen. What happens when this runs?
opts: It works, because SQLite escapes apostrophes inside values on its own
It fails, because the apostrophe in the name ends the SQL string early
It inserts the name without the apostrophe, which SQLite quietly drops
It works, but the worth is stored as text, because it came from an f string
2.why: Formatting values into SQL breaks on quotes, turns None into the word None, and allows injection. Placeholders avoid all three.
2.code:
name = "Rhea O'Dunmore"
sql = ("INSERT INTO people VALUES "
       f"('{name}', {worth})")
con.execute(sql)

3.q: Why is execute many with placeholders also faster than formatting one insert per row?
opts: Placeholders skip SQLite's type checks, so each row is written without inspection
Execute many writes the rows in parallel over several connections
SQLite parses the statement once and reuses it for every row
Formatted inserts must each be committed alone, while placeholders commit together
3.why: One prepared statement, many rows. Formatting a new string per row makes SQLite parse every one of them.

1.q: Look at the code on the screen. Why create the indexes after loading the rows rather than before?
opts: SQLite cannot create an index on a table that has no rows yet
An index created before the load would only cover the first batch of rows
Building an index once over finished data beats updating it on every insert
Indexes created early would make execute many reject rows with repeated dates
1.why: An index has to be kept up to date on each insert. Six million small updates cost far more than one build at the end.
1.code:
load_all_rows(con)
con.execute("CREATE INDEX idx_date "
            "ON rtb_all_combined (date)")
con.execute("CREATE INDEX idx_id "
            "ON rtb_all_combined (forbes_id)")

2.q: Why does the loader index the date and forbes id columns in particular?
opts: The SQL filters, groups and joins on those columns
They are the only two columns with no missing values
SQLite needs an index on every text column it is asked to sort
Together they form the primary key, which SQLite needs before it accepts inserts
2.why: Indexes pay off on the columns queries search by. Every block of the SQL filters or groups by date, and the joins use forbes id.

3.q: Look at the code on the screen. When is this trade acceptable?
opts: Always, because SQLite keeps a backup copy of the database file anyway
Only for tables with fewer than a hundred thousand rows
When the indexes are created before the load, since they protect the data
When the database is a build artifact you can rebuild from the raw files
3.why: Turning off the journal and syncing makes a crash able to corrupt the file. That is fine for a file rebuilt in seconds, and not for one that holds the only copy.
3.code:
con.execute("PRAGMA journal_mode = OFF")
con.execute("PRAGMA synchronous = OFF")

1.q: Why does every export query include an order by, even when the table was created already sorted?
opts: Without it, SQLite deliberately returns rows in a random order on every call
A table has no guaranteed row order, so only an order by fixes it
The order by also removes duplicate rows before they are written
The CSV writer needs sorted rows to write the header line correctly
1.why: Storage order can change when data grow or an index is added. Sorting by a fixed key is the only guarantee.

2.q: Look at the code on the screen. Why does the runner write floats with repr?
opts: Repr rounds to six decimals, which matches the authors' spreadsheet
The fixed six-decimal format is too slow to write for millions of rows
Repr pads every value to the same width, so the columns line up
Repr is the shortest text that reads back as exactly the same number
2.why: Six decimals loses information. Repr keeps exactly enough digits, so the file only changes when a number changes.

3.q: The year-end export sorts by date, then worth descending, then forbes id. What is the forbes id for?
opts: It breaks ties, so people with equal worth always come out in the same order
It groups each person's rows together across the seven dates
It is the primary key, which every order by is required to end with
It puts the top four first, since their ids sort before everyone else's
3.why: Two people can have the same worth on the same date. Without a tie-breaker their order could flip between runs.

1.q: Look at the code on the screen. What does the underscore merge column hold?
opts: For each row, whether it was in both tables, only the left, or only the right
The number of times each date matched, so duplicates show up as twos
True where the values in both tables are equal, and false elsewhere
The name of the table that each value column came from
1.why: Indicator adds a column with both, left only or right only. Counting its values gives the key comparison in one line.
1.code:
m = ours.merge(key, on="date", how="outer",
               indicator=True)
m["_merge"].value_counts()

2.q: Why compare a result with an answer key by merging on the key, not row by row?
opts: Merging is faster than looping over rows in pandas
A row by row check needs both tables to have exactly the same column order and names
An extra row near the top would shift every later row and fake differences
A merge also rounds the numbers, so tiny differences disappear
2.why: Aligning on the natural key makes the check immune to row order and to rows present on one side only.

3.q: Look at the code on the screen. When do these two counts mislead you?
opts: Never. With an inner join, both counts are always exact
When a date repeats on one side, since the inner join multiplies its rows
When a value column has nulls, because inner joins drop any row with a null
When the tables have different column names besides the date
3.why: Repeated keys make the inner join bigger than either side, so the subtraction can even go negative. An outer merge with an indicator counts sides directly.
3.code:
m = ours.merge(key, on="date", how="inner")
only_ours = len(ours) - len(m)
only_key = len(key) - len(m)

1.q: The checker passes numbers that differ by up to one in a million. Why not demand exact equality?
opts: The answer keys round every value to six decimal places
Python cannot compare two floats with an equals sign
It allows for small vintage gaps, such as one missing person
Adding the same numbers in a different order changes the last digits
1.why: Floating-point sums depend on the order of addition, and two programs rarely add in the same order. The real differences were about one in a trillion.

2.q: Look at the code on the screen. One person is missing from our list. Can a wider tolerance make this check pass?
opts: Yes, if the tolerance is wider than that person's worth
No. The counts differ, and counts must match exactly
Yes, because a missing person only changes the sum, not the comparison
No, because the largest difference becomes infinite whenever a row is missing
2.why: The tolerance only applies to numbers on rows both sides have. A missing person changes the count, which has no tolerance.
2.code:
TOL = 1e-6
ok = (n_ours == n_key
      and max_abs_diff <= TOL)

3.q: Suppose the R and Python exports agree to zero difference on every number, yet a few lines differ as text. How can that happen?
opts: R rounds to fifteen digits, so its numbers are slightly different
R writes missing values as N A, which the parity check reads as text
R sometimes writes seventeen digits where Python writes sixteen
R sorts ties in a different order, which moves a few lines around
3.why: R's text to number conversion is not always correctly rounded in the sixteenth digit, so the R writer sometimes needs seventeen. The doubles are identical, which is why parity compares numbers, not text.

1.q: Look at the code on the screen. Who is the exit code for?
opts: Python's own error log, which records it whenever the code is not zero
The person reading the output, since it is printed as the last line
Whatever ran the script. A shell, a Makefile or a C I job can branch on it
The next import of this module, which reads it as a cached result
1.why: Zero means success, anything else failure. Programs that run the checker can act on it without reading any text.

2.q: What is the R equivalent of sys dot exit with one?
opts: quit, with status equal to one
warning, with a message
returning one from the script's last function
invisible of one at the end of the script
2.why: quit with a status sets the exit code of an R script. A warning leaves it at zero.

3.q: Look at the code on the screen. Drill two fails. What happens?
opts: The commit runs, because the checker still printed its report
The commit runs, but git marks it as a failed commit
The shell reruns the checker until it exits with zero
Nothing is committed, since the checker exits with one
3.why: The double ampersand runs the second command only if the first exits with zero. The grader exits with one on any failing drill.

1.q: Python runs the whole SQL file with execute script. What does the R twin do instead?
opts: It calls D B I db execute once on the whole file, which runs every statement
It splits the file into statements and runs each through D B I db execute
It passes the file to the sqlite3 program with a system call
It calls Python's execute script through the reticulate package
1.why: D B I runs one statement per call, so run s q l dot R splits the text itself, skipping semicolons inside comments and strings.

2.q: Look at the code on the screen. Which R code is the closest match to this loop?
opts: read csv with n max of five thousand, then D B I db write table
D B I db write table on the whole file, which streams it in chunks by itself
A for loop over read lines, appending one row at a time
readr's read csv chunked, with a callback that appends each chunk through D B I
2.why: read csv chunked calls your function on each block of rows, like the for loop over pandas chunks. n max only reads the first rows.
2.code:
reader = pd.read_csv("rtb_sample.csv",
                     chunksize=5000)
for chunk in reader:
    chunk.to_sql("rtb", con,
                 if_exists="append",
                 index=False)

3.q: Which R check is closest to the checker's numeric test?
opts: max of abs of a minus b, at most one in a million
all equal of a and b, which also uses the largest absolute difference
identical of a and b, after rounding both to six decimals
a equals equals b, wrapped in all
3.why: The checker takes the largest absolute difference. all equal compares a mean relative difference, and identical has no tolerance at all.
